newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Deaths, torture reported since Cambodia coup.
newsitem.headline: Deaths, torture reported since Cambodia coup.

text.p: As many as 40 Cambodians have been killed since the overthrow of First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh 10 days ago but it was not clear if the killings were part of a planned purge, a diplomatic source said on Wednesday.
The source, who declined to be identified, said there was evidence of torture among some of the victims, including four bodyguards of Ranariddh's top military commander, General Nhiek Bun Chhay.
The guards were found dead with their eyes gouged out.
"It's very unclear if this is a centrally orchestrated, carefully planned purge or more dispersed -- a general uncoordinated attack on FUNCINPEC (royalist party) officials," he said.
"But even if it is the latter, it could be stopped."
He was speaking as Southeast Asian foreign ministers converged on Beijing to meet Cambodia's King Norodom Sihanouk for talks on the crisis planned for Thursday.
Sihanouk met two officials of Group of Seven nations on Tuesday and Wednesday and accused the police and army of Second Prime Minister Hun Sen of torturing and killing political opponents.
No details of the talks were made public.
A FUNCINPEC youth leader told Reuters in Phnom Penh that he and four other opposition activists were holed up in a small "safe house" in the capital.
"Of course we are afraid. People are being arrested and some have been killed," he said.
Hun Sen overthrew Ranariddh, Sihanouk's son, on July 6 after a weekend of fighting in the capital. Ranariddh left Cambodia a day before the coup.

In what political analysts see as a bid to legitimise his takeover, Hun Sen has said he wants to preserve the coalition between his Cambodian People's Party (CPP) and Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC. He said he did not want the job of first prime minister and FUNCINPEC must choose a replacement for Ranariddh.
On Wednesday, Foreign Minister Ung Huot said he was willing to accept the job as Hun Sen's new coalition partner.
"I accept to be first prime minister because I put the interests of my people and my country above everything else," Ung Huot told reporters.
"The interests of the country dictate that Cambodia must go on... We cannot wait," he said. "We've suffered too much."
An adviser to Hun Sen said the CPP accepted and would support Ung Huot's nomination.
"This is a real snow job. He (Hun Sen) is seeking legitimacy," said an Asian diplomat.
"(Ung Huot) is an ideal choice because he'll polish Hun Sen's image, nothing more, nothing less," said another diplomatic source. "He's a great face for the government...(but) he's a stooge."
Sihanouk said he was upset by reports of torture and killings.

"I am profoundly distressed at the reports that the military and members of the national police have cruelly tortured and killed without mercy their enemies after having arrested or captured them," Sihanouk said in a letter sent from Beijing to Chea Sim, the acting head of state, in Phnom Penh.
Sihanouk is receiving medical treatment in Beijing.
Hundreds of supporters and soldiers loyal to Ranariddh are believed to be in detention but military officials have denied that detainees were mistreated and said they were undergoing "re-education".

Hun Sen said on Tuesday Cambodia would have a free and fair election next May 23 as planned but the United States said Hun Sen's rhetoric in recent days, seemingly in favour of democracy, was not matched by action.

"(Hun Sen's) words are beautiful over the past 48 hours ... but whether or not he can match those words in reality with his actions is a very big test for him," U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said on Tuesday.
Ranariddh has called for resistance to Hun Sen and appealed to the international community for support but he has so far received no firm offers of help.
